name: Kaniš Merchant Archives (Old Assyrian Private Tablets)
region: Kültepe/Kaniš Lower Town, Central Anatolia, with counterpart archives at Assur
summary: The earliest large private commercial archive: roughly 23,000 clay tablets from Old Assyrian family firms at Kaniš, in which people appear as creditors, debtors, witnesses, guarantors, judges, craftspeople, and kin — a queryable social database written 1,500 years before the Silk Road.

claims.statement: The Kültepe tablets are merchant-archive documents, not isolated lexical specimens: people appear in them with roles (creditor, debtor, witness, guarantor, judge, attorney, craftsperson, kin), so the archive is a relational record of a trading society

The chronological bias is load-bearing: the vast majority of ~23,000 tablets come from Lower Town level II (c. 1970–1835 BCE); level Ib (c. 1835–1710 BCE) has yielded only around 450, so raw name counts cannot be read as cultural change without that exposure offset

Language assignment of personal names is not ethnicity: the documents are in Old Assyrian, local names are Kanišite Hittite, Luwic, Hurrian, Hattic, or unassigned, and the texts generally lump locals as nuwaʿum rather than recording self-ascription

A name is not a person: namesakes are common, a comprehensive Old Assyrian prosopography does not yet exist, and social claims from onomastics require the chain name → person → attestation → document → family/network, with ordinary legal vocabulary as a control set

evidence.source: Kültepe/Kaniš Lower Town excavations: private houses of Assyrian merchants containing tablet archives in warehouse rooms, conventionally level II c. 1970–1835 BCE and level Ib c. 1835–1710 BCE.
Larsen, M. T. (2015) Ancient Kanesh: A Merchant Colony in Bronze Age Anatolia, Cambridge University Press — appendix 'Families and Names' and index of Old Assyrian names.

Veenhof, K. R. (2020) Kültepe Texts chronique, Revue d'Assyriologie 114 — scale of personal-name material, role categories in indexes, and the continuing lack of a comprehensive Old Assyrian prosopography.

Kloekhorst, A. (2019) Kanišite Hittite: The Earliest Attested Record of Indo-European, Brill — phonological and morphological method for local personal names; dialect argument; level II vs Ib exposure.

Goedegebuure, P. (2008) Central Anatolian Languages and Language Communities in the Colony Period, in Dercksen ed., Anatolia and the Jazira during the Old Assyrian Period — language community rather than ethnicity; nuwaʿum as the Assyrian lump category.

Michel, C. (2015) professions at Kaneš; Michel, C. (2016) women and real estate. Pilot attestations: Ilališkan among Anatolian smiths (Kt 94/k 788:23) and in an 18-shekel silver loan with house pledge.

notes: Added September 2026 from anthropology/findings/kanis-name-semantics/. longevity_years=260 is the attested kārum window and will fail the 300-year bar — the same honest failure as the lathe. Do not inflate it with later Hittite archives or with the lifespan of cuneiform. replication_regions=1: Assur and the Anatolian kārums are two nodes of one carried system, not independent inventions. ethical_alignment=0.55 because the same archive that preserves family and craft also records debt, house pledge, and legal exposure. The research finding is methodological, not etymological: Ilališkan is usable because it has tablet-level roles; Atamakuni and Taripiazi are not yet statistically usable. The kārum credit system the tablets record is a downstream economic lineage, catalogued separately as karum_credit_trade. See U-C-4.
